cards.explanation: The answer is that he's deeply disturbed in his spirit. The text says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.” That's no polite frown, friends. Something in him is stirred up, and as we'll see, it gets him talking.

The answer is False. Paul doesn't keep quiet in Athens. He reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He also reasoned in the marketplace with those he met each day. I think Silas and Timothy had no idea what they'd find when they got there!

The answer is the marketplace. Besides the synagogue, Paul reasoned “…in the marketplace with those he met each day.” So his talking wasn't limited to one building. Every day he's out there, meeting people and reasoning with them.

The answer is that he's proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection. The text says they said this “…because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.” Some of them said he seemed to be advocating foreign gods. That's the reason the text gives.

The answer is True. The philosophers ask, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?” They add that he's bringing some strange notions to their ears, and they want to know what they mean. I think that's a pretty polite way to say "Okay, explain yourself."

The answer is hearing and talking about new ideas. The writer says they spent their time “…doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.” Talking and listening, that's their whole schedule, friends. If you ask me, that's a lot of ideas and a lot of ears.

The answer is that He's the God Paul now proclaims to them. Paul says, “Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.” They have an altar to an unknown God, and Paul says he's here to tell them about Him. The mystery has an answer.

The answer is False. Paul says the God who made the world is the Lord of heaven and earth and “…does not live in temples made by human hands.” I think that would've been a surprise to a city full of temples. And Paul says it right there in front of them.

The answer is that He gives everyone life and breath and everything else. Paul says God isn't served by human hands as if He needed anything, “…because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.” We're not handing Him something He lacks, friends. Everything we have comes from Him in the first place.

The answer is True. Paul says God made every nation of men and “…determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands.” So the times and the places are in His hands. Nobody's nation is an accident to Him.

The word is seek. Paul says God intended that they “…would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him…” Then he adds that God is not far from each one of us. So the search isn't a wild goose chase.
The answer is False. Paul says God “…is not far from each one of us.” He's near, not distant. That's good news for anyone who's been looking.

The answer is an image of gold or silver or stone. Paul says we should not think the Divine Being is “…like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.” We're God's offspring, so thinking He's a statue makes no sense. It's a serious point, and he makes it plainly.

The word is repent. Paul says God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, but He “…now commands all people everywhere to repent.” Notice the word everywhere, friends. That's not just for Athens or one crowd. It's for every person.

The answer is that God will judge the world with justice. Paul says God “…has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.” The day is set and the judge is appointed. That's why Paul says repent.
The answer is by raising Him from the dead. Paul says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” The proof is something God did. He raised the Man He appointed.

The answer is that some begin to mock him. When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, “…some began to mock him…” The text says some, not everyone. And right after that, we hear from others who respond differently.
The answer is True. Others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” So the same speech gets two reactions, mocking from some and interest from others. Same sermon, different ears.

The answer is Damaris. The text says some joined Paul and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, “…a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.” Think about that room, friends. Some of the crowd had just mocked Paul, and she heard the very same sermon and believed. Her name made it into the Bible, and I'd say that's a pretty good place to end up.
